God-Breathed
GOD-BREETHED
adj. (doctrine of Scripture; English rendering of theopneustos)
Direct translation of the Greek theopneustos (2 Tim 3:16): theos (God) + pneustos (breathed, from pneô, to breathe, to blow as wind); coined or adapted by Paul in 2 Timothy 3:16, first appearing in extant Greek literature in that text.

Biblical Definition

God-breathed is the English equivalent of the Greek theopneustos, Paul's defining word for the nature of Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16: “All Scripture is breathed out by God, and is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness.” The image is of breath — divine exhalation — not dictation but a more intimate and personal action: as a human speaker breathes his words forth and those words carry his thought, intention, and authority, so the Scriptures are the very breath of God, bearing His character and carrying His full authority. Peter's account complements Paul's: “no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man — but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet 1:21). The biblical writers were not passive dictating machines — their personalities, vocabularies, and historical situations are present throughout the text — but they were sovereignly overseen by the Spirit so that what they wrote was precisely what God intended. Christ Himself settled the question of Scripture's unbreakable character: “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35) — not some of it, not the doctrinally important parts, but the text itself cannot be undone. The Psalmist declared the same from the opposite direction: “Forever, O LORD, Your word is settled in heaven” (Ps 119:89). God-breathed Scripture is therefore fully authoritative in all that it affirms — history, theology, ethics, cosmology — because its ultimate author is the infinite God who cannot lie.

Webster 1828 Definition

The English rendering of the Greek theopneustos (2 Tim 3:16), signifying that the whole of Scripture proceeds from the very breath of God — fully authoritative, inerrantly true, and profitable for all that the Christian life requires.

expand to see more

GOD-BREATHED, adj. Directly translating the Greek theopneustos (2 Tim 3:16): every word of Scripture proceeds from the divine breath, carrying the full authority of the God who cannot err or deceive.

The choice of “breathed out” rather than “inspired” is significant. The Latin-rooted “inspiration” (in-spirare, to breathe into) can suggest that God breathed into already-existing human words to make them useful; theopneustos describes the Scriptures themselves as the product of divine breathing, originating from within God and emerging carrying His full authority.

God-breathed Scripture is profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training in righteousness — comprehensively sufficient for the complete equipment of the man of God. No supplementary revelation, no oral tradition, no magisterial interpretation is needed to complete what the text lacks; the text does not lack.

The doctrine stands or falls with Christ's own testimony: “the Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). He who is the Truth (John 14:6) could not appeal to a text He knew to be in error; His appeal to Scripture as unbreakable is the definitive testimony.

The Reformed confessional standard (1689 LBCF 1.1–10) unfolds what theopneustos means practically: Scripture is its own interpreter (analogia Scripturae), sufficient and perspicuous, standing as the supreme standard over all human tradition and ecclesiastical pronouncement.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16 — "All Scripture is breathed out by God, and is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, for training in righteousness —"

2 Peter 1:21 — "For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man — but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit."

John 10:35 — "If He called them 'gods,' to whom the word of God came — and the Scripture cannot be broken —"

Psalm 119:89 — "Forever, O LORD, Your word is settled in heaven."

Modern Corruption

The historical-critical method treats Scripture as a human document subject to correction by analysis of sources and redactors; neo-orthodox theology treats Scripture as merely becoming the Word of God in moments of encounter — both deny the God-breathed character Paul asserts.

expand to see more

The historical-critical method, which became dominant in German universities in the 18th and 19th centuries (Eichhorn, Wellhausen, Strauss), begins with the methodological assumption that the biblical text must be analyzed as any other ancient document — by source analysis, redaction criticism, and form criticism. This is not neutral scholarship; it is a prior commitment to treating the text as not God-breathed. When historical-critical scholarship assigns authorship to “Deutero-Isaiah” or the “Priestly source,” it is presupposing that the text could not have been supernaturally produced. The MOOP Dictionary does not grant historical criticism its epistemological starting point; it holds Scripture's own claim of God-breathed origin as the interpretive beginning.

Neo-orthodox theology (Barth, Brunner) attempted a middle path: Scripture “becomes” the Word of God in the moment of existential encounter, but is not identical to the Word of God as text. The result is a Scripture that is instrumentally useful for the church but formally uncertain — one that can contain errors and still function as a vehicle of divine encounter. Against this, the Reformed tradition holds: Scripture does not merely become the Word of God in the moment of reading; it is the Word of God in its very written form, because it was God-breathed in its composition.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek theos (God) + pneustos (breathed, from pneô — to breathe, to blow); in 2 Tim 3:16, the compound theopneustos is Paul's coinage for the divine origin of all Scripture.

expand to see more

Greek theos — God; the first element signals divine agency and authority as the ultimate source of the text.

Greek pneustos (from pneô) — breathed, blown; used for the breath of wind, the breath of life, and here for the divine exhalation that produces Scripture.

Greek pneûma — breath, spirit, wind; the Spirit who carries the writers (2 Pet 1:21) is the same Spirit whose breath produces Scripture, linking inspiration and pneumatology.

Latin inspirare — to breathe into; the Latin translation that produced the English “inspiration,” which can mislead by suggesting God breathed into existing human material rather than breathing out the text itself.

Hebrew neshamah — breath; used for the divine breath that gave Adam life (Gen 2:7); Paul's theopneustos echoes this life-breath imagery, suggesting Scripture carries the same animating divine life.

Usage

"The God-breathed character of Scripture is the foundation of all biblical preaching: the preacher who reads the text reads what God Himself has said — not a merely human witness to what God once said."

"It grounds inerrancy without imposing dictation: God breathed out Scripture through human writers whose personalities were not suppressed, but whose words were exactly what He intended."

"Where the God-breathed character of Scripture is denied or qualified, preaching loses its authority, ethics loses its absolute ground, and the church loses the standard that stands above every tradition and council."
